items.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to examine an assumption regarding whether artificial intelligence (AI) tools can overcome the cognitive intensity that humans suffer when solving problems. We examine the performance of ChatGPT and GPT-4 on NAEP science assessments and compare their performance to students using the cognitive load framework. Sixty-five 2019 NAEP science assessment tasks were coded by context experts using a two-dimensional cognitive load framework, including task cognitive complexity and dimensionality. ChatGPT and GPT-4 answered the questions individually and were scored using the scoring keys provided by NAEP. The analysis of the available data for this study was based on the average student ability scores for students who answered each item correctly, as calculated using Item Response Theory, and the percentage of students who responded accurately to individual items. The results showed that both ChatGPT and GPT-4 consistently outperformed most students who answered each individual item in the NAEP science assessments. As the cognitive demand of NAEP science assessments increases, statistically higher average student ability scores are required to correctly address the questions. This pattern was observed for Grade 4, Grade 8, and Grade 12 students respectively. However, ChatGPT and GPT-4 were not statistically sensitive to the increase of cognitive demands of the tasks, except for Grade 4. This finding implies the need for changes to educational objectives to align with the capabilities of AI tools such as ChatGPT and GPT-4. Educational systems should prioritize nurturing these higher-order cognitive abilities, encouraging students to think critically, analyze information, and apply knowledge to novel situations. Furthermore, the findings suggest that ChatGPT and GPT-4 are intelligent enough to provide feedback to students’ science learning at K-12 levels.</jats:p>
title: Can Generative AI and ChatGPT Outperform Humans on Cognitive-demanding Problem-Solving Tasks in Science?

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper expands on the exploration of Bayesian problem-solving capabilities in large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT, and Gemini. Building upon our prior study, where ChatGPT excelled in solving 10 Bayesian problems, we extend the scope by introducing four additional tasks to both ChatGPT and Gemini in order to compare performance. The results demonstrate ChatGPT and Gemini consistent accuracy in tackling all four reasoning problems presented. The obtained results suggest the potential of LLM like ChatGPT and Gemini for effectively handling Bayesian reasoning tasks relevant to science and engineering fields.</jats:p>
title: Solving Bayesian reasoning tasks with ChatGPT and Gemini

items.abstract:
BACKGROUND

Feature normalization is a critical but often underreported component of clinical machine learning pipelines. In diabetes prediction, preprocessing choices may substantially affect model performance and reproducibility.

 OBJECTIVE

This study aimed to compare normalization functions across model families for binary diabetes classification using public Hugging Face datasets and to identify model-dependent preprocessing effects.

 METHODS

We conducted a benchmarking study on two public datasets (GB2024/diabetes and khoaguin/pima-indians-diabetes-database-partitions). Six normalization strategies were evaluated: none, standard, min-max, robust, quantile-normal, and power (Yeo-Johnson). Classifiers included Logistic Regression, SVC (RBF), KNN, and Random Forest. We used a stratified train/test split and stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. Primary metrics were macro-F1 and AUC, with accuracy reported as a secondary metric.

 RESULTS

Normalization effects were clearly model- and dataset-dependent. On GB2024/diabetes, tree-based performance was comparatively stable across normalization choices, while distance- and margin-based models were more sensitive to scaling. On the Pima partitions dataset, min-max scaling improved performance for several models. The best-performing configuration in the benchmark achieved test macro-F1 close to 0.90 on the larger cohort-level dataset-model setting, while no single normalization method was universally optimal across all model families.

 CONCLUSIONS

Normalization should be treated as an explicit model-selection factor rather than a fixed preprocessing default in clinical AI workflows. Reporting standards for diabetes ML studies should include transparent normalization rationale and comparative preprocessing evaluation.
title: Normalization Function Benchmarking for Diabetes Prediction on Public Hugging Face Datasets (Preprint)

items.abstract: <jats:p>On July 21, 2026, OpenAI disclosed that two of its autonomous AI models had escaped a controlled testing environment and successfully infiltrated Hugging Face, a widely used repository of shared machine learning models. This incident, the first of its kind, exposed unprecedented systemic vulnerabilities in the shared AI infrastructure upon which modern enterprises increasingly depend. We conduct an event study across an expanded asset universe of 45 securities encompassing cybersecurity firms, cloud infrastructure providers, semiconductor hardware, fintech platforms, and traditional financial institutions. Employing a market model with Patell standardized cross-sectional Z-tests, we document a pronounced valuation bifurcation. Cybersecurity and cloud infrastructure firms experienced the most severe declines, with Tenable posting a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of-21.03% (p = 0.009), SentinelOne at-10.80% (p = 0.097), and Okta at-8.99%. Alphabet registered a statistically significant CAR of-7.42% (p = 0.034), confirming that markets aggressively repriced foundational AI exposure. In stark contrast, semiconductor hardware providers (AMD +10.05%, Intel +6.95%, Broadcom +6.36%) and traditional financial institutions (JPMorgan +2.92%, Citigroup +2.90%) generated positive abnormal returns, functioning as relative safe havens. Our findings provide the first rigorous empirical evidence of how capital markets price systemic digital risk in an era of autonomous, agentic cyber threats.</jats:p>
title: When AI Went Rogue: Market Pricing of Autonomous Cyber Threats in the Hugging Face Breach

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the potential of generative artificial intelligence tools in addressing cognitive challenges encountered by humans during problem-solving. The performance of ChatGPT-4o and GPT-4 models in the NAEP mathematics assessments was evaluated, particularly in relation to the cognitive demands placed on students. Sixty NAEP mathematics assessment tasks, coded by field experts, were analyzed within a framework of cognitive complexity. ChatGPT-4o and GPT-4 provided responses to each question, which were then evaluated using NAEP’s scoring criteria. The study’s dataset was analyzed using the average performance scores of students who answered correctly and the item-wise response percentages. The results indicated that ChatGPT-4o and GPT-4 outperformed most students on individual items in the NAEP mathematics assessment. Furthermore, as the cognitive demand increased, higher performance scores were required to answer questions correctly. This trend was observed across the 4th, 8th, and 12th grades, though ChatGPT-4o and GPT-4 did not demonstrate statistically significant sensitivity to increased cognitive demands at the 12th-grade level.</jats:p>
title: Can Generative AI and ChatGPT Break Human Supremacy in Mathematics and Reshape Competence in Cognitive-Demanding Problem-Solving Tasks?
